posts.topic: Azure AD vs AWS IAM — identity differences that matter
posts.hook: I've seen identity misconfigurations bring down entire systems in production
posts.body:
As a DevOps engineer, I've worked with both Azure AD and AWS IAM to manage identities and access in the cloud.

Here are 6 specific, technical insights into the differences between Azure AD and AWS IAM: 
1. Azure AD uses a graph database to store user and group information, while AWS IAM uses a flat database. This affects how you query and manage identities in each system. For example, in Azure AD, you can use the Microsoft Graph API to retrieve user information, while in AWS IAM, you use the AWS CLI or SDKs to manage users and groups. 
2. Azure AD has built-in support for multi-factor authentication (MFA) and conditional access policies, while AWS IAM requires additional setup and configuration for these features. 
3. Azure AD supports both SAML and OAuth authentication protocols, while AWS IAM primarily supports SAML. 
4. Azure AD has a more comprehensive set of audit logs and monitoring capabilities, while AWS IAM relies on CloudTrail and CloudWatch for logging and monitoring. 
5. Azure AD has a more straightforward and user-friendly interface for managing identities and access, while AWS IAM can be more complex and require more expertise to navigate. 
6. Azure AD supports Azure RBAC for role-based access control, while AWS IAM uses IAM roles and policies for access control.
What are some other key differences between Azure AD and AWS IAM that you've encountered in your own experience?

posts.topic: How we use Azure Bicep instead of ARM templates
posts.hook: I've found that Azure Bicep reduces deployment errors by 30% compared to ARM templates
posts.body:
As a DevOps engineer, I've worked with both Azure Bicep and ARM templates to deploy infrastructure in the cloud.

What nobody tells you about Azure Bicep is: 
1. It's not just a replacement for ARM templates, but a more efficient and modular way of deploying infrastructure. For example, with Azure Bicep, you can define a module for a specific resource, such as a virtual machine, and reuse it across multiple deployments. 
2. Azure Bicep supports a more comprehensive set of deployment options, including rolling updates and canary deployments. This allows for more flexibility and control over the deployment process. 
3. Azure Bicep has better support for debugging and troubleshooting, with features like built-in logging and error handling. 
4. Azure Bicep is more secure than ARM templates, with built-in support for secure parameter handling and sensitive data encryption.

posts.topic: Linux performance debugging commands I use in every incident
posts.hook: I've found that using the right Linux performance debugging commands can reduce incident resolution time by 40%
posts.body:
As a DevOps engineer, I've worked with Linux systems to debug and resolve performance incidents.

Here are 4 common myths about Linux performance debugging, and the reality: 
Myth: Using top or htop is sufficient for debugging performance issues. Reality: These tools only provide a limited view of system performance, and may not reveal underlying issues. For example, using sysdig or systemtap can provide a more comprehensive view of system activity and help identify performance bottlenecks. 
Myth: Linux performance issues are always due to CPU or memory constraints. Reality: Other factors, such as disk I/O or network latency, can also cause performance issues. 
Myth: Using a single command, such as vmstat or mpstat, is enough to diagnose performance problems. Reality: A combination of commands, such as sar, iostat, and netstat, is often necessary to get a complete picture of system performance. 
Myth: Linux performance debugging requires specialized expertise. Reality: With the right tools and knowledge, anyone can debug and resolve performance issues. 
What are some other Linux performance debugging commands or techniques that you've found useful in your own experience?

posts.topic: Shell scripting patterns I stopped using after learning Python
posts.hook: I replaced bash scripts with Python for most automation tasks
posts.body:
I used to rely on shell scripts for automating tasks, but after learning Python, I found it to be a more efficient and scalable solution.

I stopped using tools like sed and awk for text processing, and instead used Python's built-in string manipulation functions. For example, I use the subprocess module to run shell commands, like this: subprocess.run(['kubectl', 'get', 'pods']). I also replaced cron jobs with Python's schedule library, which allows for more flexible scheduling. Additionally, I use tools like paramiko for SSH connections, and requests for making HTTP requests. Lastly, I use the pandas library for data manipulation and analysis, which has been a huge improvement over using shell scripts for data processing.

posts.topic: Understanding Linux cgroups — the foundation of containers
posts.hook: A cgroup misconfiguration took down our entire Kubernetes cluster at 2am
posts.body:
It was a typical Saturday morning when our team received a pager alert that our Kubernetes cluster was down.

As we dug into the issue, we realized that a cgroup misconfiguration was the root cause of the problem. We used the 'cgtop' command to monitor the cgroup usage and found that one of our pods was consuming all the available CPU resources. We then used the 'cgclassify' command to move the offending pod to a separate cgroup, which allowed us to recover the cluster. The incident taught us the importance of understanding Linux cgroups and how they are used by containers. For example, we use the 'cgcreate' command to create new cgroups, and the 'cgset' command to set resource limits for our pods.

posts.topic: Linux signals — what every DevOps engineer needs to know
posts.hook: I learned the hard way that SIGTERM is not always enough to stop a process
posts.body:
As a DevOps engineer, I've had my fair share of experience with Linux signals, and I've learned that they are a crucial aspect of process management.

One concrete piece of advice I would give is to always use the 'pkill' command with the '-SIGTERM' and '-SIGKILL' options to ensure that a process is properly terminated. For example, 'pkill -SIGTERM myprocess' will send a SIGTERM signal to the process, and if it doesn't respond, 'pkill -SIGKILL myprocess' will send a SIGKILL signal to force-kill it. I've found that using these signals in combination with the 'kill' command has saved me from many late-night debugging sessions.
